> *** Re: Issue [#11523](https://github.com/whatwg/html/issues/11523) Removal of XSLT from the web platform
> 
> As I was debugging an XSLT Stylesheet for my GitHub project last week I received the notice from GitHub in the Browser Diagnostic Tools that XSLT was deprecated and will be removed from browsers in 2026. Since that time I have been trying to understand the process that led to this decision, and the path forward for me, and likely others like me. I am still looking for solid answers.
> 
> Most concerning of all is that this issue has not been advertised or discussed in a public forum. GitHub knows the makeup of my project as shown below... I should have been notified in October, long before this decision was finalized.
> 
> Discussion... Client Side XSLT is the perfect solution for what I am doing. Enabled by static html pages on GitHub, it's browser agnostic and it's standards based.
> 
> The rationale presented in "Should we remove XSLT from the web platform? [#11523](https://github.com/whatwg/html/issues/11523) [(https://github.com/whatwg/html/issues/11523)](url) sound like arguments of convenience. They do not present a business value argument. They are not compelling.
> 
> Downloads argument...** [#11523](https://github.com/whatwg/html/issues/11523) says..."a significant [decline](https://chromestatus.com/metrics/feature/timeline/popularity/78) in the use of client-side XSLT. Its role within the web browser has been largely superseded by JavaScript-based technologies such as JSON+React." Indeed there are additional options, but that is not a rationale. By that metric, my project is worthless... it contains 4.6% CSS, 5.8% XSLT, 88.8% JavaScript, and 0.8% other. 99% of the JavaScript is loaded from open source. 100% of the XSLT is coded by me. The rationale did not quantify the impact of removing an option away with short notice and no a migration path. The impact to me is that the project becomes a doorstop if/when XSLT goes away. Likely others are severely impacted as well.
> 
> Security Vulnerabilities argument... CVE.ORG shows 112 total registered vulnerabilities for XSLT for all recorded time. There were none in 2026 and five in 2025. In contrast, 7687 vulnerabilities have been registered for JavaScript, with more than 50 to date in 2026. So from that basis, logic supports removing JavaScript...
> 
> The business value argument needs to include: cost, time, and loss of function.
> 
> Ironically, my small GitHub project is security related (which is listed as an issue for eliminating XSLT. [https://jjwhitmore.github.io/SE-workbench/ ](url). The tools allow the users to investigate a range of security issues and perspectives on their local platform. The tools easily show 36 variants of JavaScript attacks. Google Analytics shows that the project has been used by more than 450 users from 40 countries.
> 
> For your consideration, and the consideration of the Issue [#11523](https://github.com/whatwg/html/issues/11523) collaborators... my suggestion would be to pause the deprecation of XSLT until the true impact can be investigated, look into whether XSLT can be packaged browser plug-ins, run the plug-in in a sandbox, and then focus on bulletproofing JavaScript.

I do not see that this is a duplicate issue.

I was prevented from commenting on the original issue because I am not listed as a collaborator.

Please allow me to post me comments to the original issue, or reopen the current issue.

Thank you.

HL7 CCDA is based on XML, hence it uses XSL in a huge range of scenarios in health IT, but particularly in web based systems that are not public (because its health care data) - impossible to 'analyse' the proportion.

What is HL7? - the largest open standard for health care data interchange, used internationally and particularly the USA.
What is CCDA? - an XML based document for patient data interchange that US health care providers are legally required to provide to patients on discharge.

If you remove XSL from browsers you will break an unknown number of applications and systems, effecting millions of vulnerable patients. If you want to fix the problems with XSL, fix the problems in the standard.

Why am I posting here? - If you label a post as duplicate, the functionality in the duplicate needs to exist in the original (or its clearly not a duplicate).

Maybe we could link to where to direct comments to chromium, who volunteered to try this?  It does seem like we _want_ to know effects, but if the original issue is shut to non-collaborators, where do they provide it? / Perhaps @mfreed7 can help advise?

A superficial analysis of the presence of XSL on the public facing web is hardly enough to know the effects of removing it from private web-based applications, of which there are many. These are based on open and government standards, which have taken decades to establish.

Sorry it seems that way to you. That's not **actually how it is** though - I do care about the platform, and I do care about the pain of this deprecation. I actively read all of the comments and try to glean if there are real issues that I can address. Or situations that can't be overcome via the polyfill. And I'm doing everything I can do minimize the pain. But I believe (along with the other members of WHATWG) that the removal of XSLT is in the general best interest of the platform. Using a "greatest good for the greatest number of people" metric, that is. In this general debate, it's unfortunately very common that people raise issues but then don't respond to my followup conversation about them. For example:

> But can you say why the polyfill isn't an option for your project?

Following your excellent point, I began checking out polyfill to figure out what would be involved to determine whether polyfill is applicable to my project. I loaded the XSLT polyfill chrome extension. 

In short order I found out that it doesn't work with browsers having native XSLT, which implies that I can't provide an answer until after XSLT is removed.  

I also found blogs that say what has already said, and ask the question... "do you really want to do client-side processing when is so much better?" 

A couple of questions...
1. is there a way to test polyfill functionality without waiting for XSLT to be removed? If not, then your request for feedback is mute.  

2. Is there a list of XSLT functions and capabilities that you know will break without a solution like polyfill? this would be more productive than sending the world on a waste of time treasure hunt to reconfirm what is already known. 
 -

> > But can you say why the polyfill isn't an option for your project?

Maybe it is - but it is an almost 10 year old project that has been forked many times. 

But my little project is beside the point - HL7 CCDA is an international standard, with a huge number of systems integrating health data, largely not public facing. You have no way of assessing the impact of this change on them without a study that would involve actively asking the user base.

Then don't ask questions that have no right of reply (yes, I know why its locked, but that doesn't change the fact that I can't respond)

Now that I have a better lay of the land, I am offering my opinion for everyone on the thread to consider.  I know that if / when my application stops working the world will go on.  I am suggesting that the rationale to quit XSLT without an evolutionary plan is problematic.  Here is why...     

My takeaway from the discussion is that the decision has been made, and the XSLT V1 function is going away, and there will be no replacement.  The drive to eliminate XSLT is rationalized by the perception of limited use of XSLT v JavaScript, and available alternatives for some unknown percentage of solutions, i.e., JavaScript and polyfill.  My sense is that eliminating XSLT is more about business pressures than about the value and vulnerabilities of the XSLT software. The complication is that what was an open source project is entangled with business issues, and XSLT is one of the foundations of the open Internet and distributed computing.  

The discussion here and in #11523 point to 2 use cases that appear to be partially addressed by polyfill,: 
1. format and rendering of specialized streams in browsers such as RSS Feeds  
2. format and rendering of structured documents and HTML pages in browsers.

My use case is different. Based on my reading it cannot be solved with polyfill.  I do not think that my use case is a one-off.  My use case involves transformation and formatting of XML data that is rendered in browsers using open source DataTables [ https://datatables.net/ ] . 

A quick Internet search shows there are in the range of 255,000+ DataTables customers. Some pretty big and important names and websites. DataTables uses XSLT. There are ten pages of XSLT related examples and forum posts on the DataTables website. In my opinion, if there is any level of XSLT use by the 250,000+ DataTables customers, there could be a significant denial of client services for governments, businesses, academia, etc., on the day that XSLT is turned off in Chrome, FireFox and Safari... 

FYI, my GitHub project uses DataTables to render a tabular view of XML data that has been transformed into cells of hybrid text / using XSLT.  The value of DataTables is that the user can examine, manipulate and export the table data locally, and privately. Polyfill can't do this. Server-side computing can't provide full user interactivity for a table size for one of my tools is about 2000 rows and 25 columns, or about 50,000 cells.  The project is 10% XSLT and CSS, and 90% JavaScript.  

As someone who has dealt with business strategy and product plans in the past, it seems risky to potentially break functionality for 255,000+ organizations, governments and websites around the world. A more strategic approach to solving the Chromium business problem would be to find an independent open source project to own and maintain XSLT, then Chromium could easily decide whether to include XSLT functionality in the browser in the future.

> In short order I found out that it doesn't work with browsers having native XSLT, which implies that I can't provide an answer until after XSLT is removed.

In Chrome at least, you can easily turn it off at `chrome://flags/#xslt`. 

> Then don't ask questions that have no right of reply (yes, I know why its locked, but that doesn't change the fact that I can't respond)

If you're able to elaborate on why the polyfill can't solve your use case, we can discuss. The polyfill attempts (modulo any bugs, which I'd like to fix) to reproduce the two functions provided by browsers today: XSLT processing instructions, and the XSLTProcessor API. If your existing use case uses one of those two things, it should fall into the use cases it supports.

I'm not sure how DataTables is affected. From their home page: "DataTables is a Javascript HTML table enhancing library". I searched around and could not find any references to it using XSLT - can you point me to the relevant documentation for that?

I'll stop responding to this thread now, since I think it's run its course. As I said above, if you have issues with the polyfill, please feel free to file them.

I disagree with your assertion that the issue of removing XSLT has run its course. 

I continue to work on the due diligence that the issue requires. I have found that the alternatives to direct XSLT support you suggested (polyfill and saxon-js) do not appear to work for my solution: 
- **Polyfill** displays nothing, with no error indications, and no documentation. I opened an item [ https://github.com/mfreed7/xslt_extension/issues/3 ] on Feb 18 as you advised, and you have not responded. 
- **Saxon-js** appears to turn my interactive DataTable into a static web page, which is worthless. 

Beyond the refactoring and experimenting, I have other experiences to share... 
- My Security Engineering project has been accepted as a NIST Community Resource Tool for Cybersecurity, which is good for now, but it will cease to work as a consequences of the plan to remove XSLT.    
- I was recently informed that my medical provider is in the process of migrating to new portal technology.  I was advised that I should download a copy of my medical records. When I unzipped the file, I found that all the records are in XML format, with an XSL stylesheet. I quickly realized that I will lose capability to view my medical record history as a consequence.  I am personally dealing with the consequences of the plan to remove XSLT. 
- I contacted the W3C to inquire about their view of XSLT support. I found two things: My contact indicated that W3C is aware of the plan, and is monitoring. I also found that Google is a W3C member, and that as stated on the W3C website, Google's mission is to organize the world’s information and make it universally accessible and useful. On he surface, it seems that removing XSLT somehow diminishes that mission.    

This information, along with the responses to this GitHub issue highlighting known impacts to current solutions in financial, telecom and healthcare industries, reinforces the point that the decision to deprecate XSLT is based on incomplete rationale and unknown impacts. 

All that being said, I do see that the plan to deprecate XSLT is proceeding, i.e., a recent posting says that Chrome XSLT flag is being reset to default of "disabled" possibly this week.  

In a world where there are so many significant things happening, it seems curious that a stable, useful and benign programming capability such as XSLT is targeted for elimination. There must be something more going on... 

Your "I'll stop responding to this thread now" comment speaks volumes.
